guide.summary: Unit 3 runs from Reconstruction through the early 20th century: how freedpeople built lives and institutions, how Reconstruction's gains were rolled back by Jim Crow, debates over strategy among Black leaders, the Great Migration, the Harlem Renaissance, and Black Americans' struggles for rights during the world wars.

sections.heading: Reconstruction and its reversal
sections.body: After 1865, freedpeople reunited families, founded churches and schools, and sought land. The Freedmen's Bureau (1865) aided education and labor contracts; many HBCUs date from this era. Southern states passed Black Codes to restrict freedpeople's labor and movement. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) established birthright citizenship and equal protection, and the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote based on race. Black men voted and held office: Hiram Revels became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870. Without land redistribution, most freedpeople became sharecroppers trapped in debt. Violence by groups such as the Ku Klux Klan and the end of Reconstruction (1877) let white Southern Democrats regain control. Disenfranchisement through poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and white primaries followed, and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld 'separate but equal.' Some sought new homes, such as the Exodusters who moved to Kansas in 1879.

sections.heading: Strategies and debates
sections.body: Ida B. Wells investigated lynching (Southern Horrors, 1892), showing that it was used to terrorize Black communities, often over economic competition, rather than to punish crime. Booker T. Washington's 1895 Atlanta Exposition address urged Black Southerners to focus on industrial education and economic progress and to accept social separation for the time being. W. E. B. Du Bois, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), criticized this for accepting disenfranchisement, called for full civil and political rights and higher education (the 'Talented Tenth'), and described 'double consciousness,' the experience of seeing oneself through the eyes of a racist society. Du Bois helped lead the Niagara Movement (1905) and the NAACP (1909), which used lawsuits and publicity. Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) promoted Black pride, economic self-reliance, and Pan-Africanism, including a 'Back to Africa' vision. Entrepreneurs such as Madam C. J. Walker built businesses, and Tulsa's Greenwood district ('Black Wall Street') thrived until a white mob destroyed it in 1921.

sections.heading: Migration, culture, and war
sections.body: In the Great Migration (about 1910–1970), roughly six million Black Southerners moved to Northern and Western cities to escape Jim Crow and seek work, transforming American cities and politics. The Harlem Renaissance (1920s–1930s) celebrated Black culture: Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925), poetry by Langston Hughes and Claude McKay, Zora Neale Hurston's writing on Black Southern life and folklore, and jazz and blues. Black soldiers served in segregated units in both world wars; returning veterans faced violence, as in the Red Summer of 1919. In World War II, the Pittsburgh Courier's 'Double V' campaign called for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home. A. Philip Randolph's threatened March on Washington pushed Roosevelt to ban discrimination in defense industries (1941), and Truman's Executive Order 9981 (1948) began desegregating the military.

keyTakeaways: Freedpeople built churches, schools, families, and political power.
The 14th and 15th Amendments were undermined by violence and Jim Crow.
Washington, Du Bois, Wells, and Garvey offered different strategies.
The Great Migration reshaped where and how Black Americans lived.
The Harlem Renaissance asserted Black cultural identity.
Wartime service fueled demands for rights at home.
commonMistakes: Saying Washington opposed all civil rights; he emphasized economic progress first and quietly funded some legal challenges.
Confusing Black Codes (1865–66) with later Jim Crow laws.
Treating Reconstruction as a failure with no lasting gains (amendments, institutions).
Placing the Harlem Renaissance after World War II.
Mixing up Garvey's Pan-Africanism with the NAACP's integration strategy.
examTips: Know the Washington–Du Bois debate cold; it appears in many forms.
Use Wells to show investigative journalism as activism.
Link the Great Migration to later Northern political power and civil rights activism.

practice.prompt:
Source 1 (summary): In his 1895 Atlanta Exposition address, Booker T. Washington urged Black Southerners to build economic security through farming, trades, and industrial education, and suggested that demands for social equality could wait.

Source 2 (summary): In The Souls of Black Folk (1903), W. E. B. Du Bois argued that Washington's approach accepted disenfranchisement and second-class citizenship, and insisted on the right to vote, civil equality, and higher education.

Answer A, B, C, and D.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe one way Du Bois's argument in Source 2 differs from Washington's.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain one historical development in the 1890s that shaped this debate.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how another individual or organization of the period pursued a different strategy for Black advancement.

rubric.description: Economic self-help and vocational education first; postpone agitation for social equality.
Du Bois demanded immediate political and civil rights and higher/liberal arts education.
E.g., Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), Southern disenfranchisement laws, rising lynching, the end of Reconstruction.
E.g., Ida B. Wells's anti-lynching journalism; the NAACP's legal strategy; Garvey's UNIA and Pan-Africanism; Exodusters' migration.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Washington argued that Black Southerners should focus on economic progress through industrial education and skilled labor, building wealth and respect first while setting aside demands for social equality.

B. Du Bois rejected waiting; he argued that Black Americans must demand the vote and equal civil rights now, and that college education was needed to develop leaders.

C. In the 1890s, Southern states disenfranchised Black voters through poll taxes and literacy tests, and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld segregation. These setbacks made Washington's accommodation seem practical to some and unacceptable to Du Bois.

D. Ida B. Wells used investigative journalism to expose lynching and urged boycotts and migration from Memphis, directly confronting racial violence rather than accommodating it.
